# Confidence intervals

A point estimate does not say how far it might fall from the parameter. A confidence interval attaches a long-run coverage probability to a random interval built from the sample. After the sample is observed the endpoints are numbers. The confidence, say 95%, is a property of the procedure that produced them, not a probability that the parameter lies in that particular interval.

That last distinction is the same one drawn for a [credible interval](bayes-01-foundations.qmd#def-bayesian-credible-interval). A credible interval puts the probability on the parameter, given the data. A confidence interval puts the probability on the interval, given the parameter.

The normal, chi-squared, $t$ and $F$ laws used below are defined in [Statistical inference](inf-01-statistical-inference.qmd), together with the [normal sample theorem](inf-01-statistical-inference.qmd#thm-normal-sample-theorem) that links them to a sample. The binomial intervals rest on the [central limit theorem](prob-05-transforms-and-limits.qmd#thm-central-limit-theorem).

## From a standard error to an interval

A company introduced new safety measures. In the 50 months since, lost working hours averaged 91 per month, with bias-corrected sample standard deviation 14.1. In the 50 months before, they averaged 108, with standard deviation 14.3. The estimate of the change in mean is $91-108=-17$ hours per month. How accurate is it?

Model the two runs of months as independent samples, with means $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ and a common variance $\sigma^2$. The estimator $\overline X_1-\overline X_2$ is unbiased for $\mu_1-\mu_2$, with variance

$$
\Var(\overline X_1-\overline X_2)=\frac{\sigma^2}{50}+\frac{\sigma^2}{50}=\frac{\sigma^2}{25}.
$$

Estimating $\sigma^2$ by the pooled variance $s_p^2=(49\times14.1^2+49\times14.3^2)/98=14.20^2$ gives a standard error of $14.20/5=2.84$. A common way to report this is $-17\pm2.84$, or $-17\pm2\times2.84$.

What probability goes with "estimate plus or minus a standard error"? Take the simplest case, $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ independent and $\Normal(\mu,1)$. Then $\sqrt n(\overline X-\mu)$ is standard normal, and

$$
\Pr\bigl(\overline X-n^{-1/2}<\mu<\overline X+n^{-1/2}\bigr)=\Pr\bigl(-1<\sqrt n(\overline X-\mu)<1\bigr)=2\Phi(1)-1=0.683.
$$

Plus or minus one standard error covers $\mu$ only 68% of the time. Plus or minus two covers it with probability $2\Phi(2)-1=0.954$. Choosing the multiplier is choosing the coverage.

## Coverage

::: {#def-confidence-interval .definition}
## Confidence interval

Let $L$ and $U$ be statistics. The random interval $(L,U)$ is a confidence interval for $\theta$ with confidence $1-\alpha$ when

$$
\Pr_\theta(L<\theta<U)=1-\alpha
$$

for every $\theta$. A one-sided interval leaves one endpoint infinite.

:::

The observed interval $(l,u)$, computed from the data, is still called the confidence interval. Smaller $\alpha$ means a wider interval, and a very wide interval says little. The usual choices are $0.01$, $0.05$ and $0.10$, that is 99%, 95% and 90% confidence. When the coverage holds only for large samples, the interval is approximate.

![Forty samples of size 10 from $\Normal(10,1)$, each with its 95% $t$ interval for $\mu$. Thirty-eight cover $\mu=10$. The two in red miss it. In repeated sampling about 5% of such intervals miss, and nothing in an interval's own data shows whether it is one of them.](../figures/inf-coverage.pdf){#fig-inf-coverage}

Suppose a 90% interval for $\mu$ comes out as $(9.5,10.5)$. It is tempting to write $\Pr(9.5<\mu<10.5)=0.9$, but $\mu$ is a fixed number, so that probability is either $0$ or $1$, and which one is unknown. The $0.9$ belongs to the random interval $(L,U)$ before the data arrive. An urn holds 90 white balls and 10 black. Draw one without looking. You are fairly sure it is white, and you hold it in a closed hand. That is the right degree of confidence that $(9.5,10.5)$ contains $\mu$.

::: {#def-pivot .definition}
## Pivot

A pivot is a function $h(\vect X;\theta)$ of the data and the parameter whose distribution does not depend on any unknown parameter.

:::

Every interval in this chapter is built the same way. Find a pivot. Choose its quantiles $h_{\alpha/2}$ and $h_{1-\alpha/2}$, so that

$$
\Pr\bigl(h_{\alpha/2}<h(\vect X;\theta)<h_{1-\alpha/2}\bigr)=1-\alpha.
$$

Rearrange the inequality to isolate $\theta$. The rearrangement does not change the event, so the coverage is still $1-\alpha$. The pivot must not depend on unknown parameters, or its quantiles cannot be computed. That is why the $t$ statistic, which replaces $\sigma$ by $s$, is a pivot, and $\sqrt n(\overline X-\mu)/\sigma$ with unknown $\sigma$ is not.

## One normal sample

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent and $\Normal(\mu,\sigma^2)$.

If $\sigma$ is known,

$$
Z=\frac{\overline X-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}
$$

is standard normal. Writing $z_{1-\alpha/2}$ for the standard normal quantile of order $1-\alpha/2$,

$$
\overline X\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}
$$

is a confidence interval for $\mu$ with confidence $1-\alpha$. For 95%, $z_{0.975}=1.960$.

If $\sigma$ is unknown, replace it by $s$. The pivot is no longer normal.

::: {#thm-one-sample-t .theorem}
## One-sample t pivot

If $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are independent and $\Normal(\mu,\sigma^2)$, then

$$
T=\frac{\overline X-\mu}{s/\sqrt n}
$$

has a Student $t$ distribution with $n-1$ degrees of freedom. A Student variable with $m$ degrees of freedom is $Z/\sqrt{V/m}$ where $Z$ is standard normal, $V$ is chi-squared with $m$ degrees of freedom, and $Z$ and $V$ are independent.

:::

To see this, divide top and bottom by $\sigma/\sqrt n$:

$$
T=\frac{(\overline X-\mu)/(\sigma/\sqrt n)}{\sqrt{\dfrac{(n-1)s^2/\sigma^2}{n-1}}}=\frac{Z}{\sqrt{V/(n-1)}}.
$$

By the normal sample theorem, $Z$ is standard normal, $V=(n-1)s^2/\sigma^2$ is $\chi^2_{n-1}$, and they are independent, because $Z$ depends on $\overline X$ alone and $V$ on $s^2$ alone. The unknown $\sigma$ has cancelled, so $T$ is a pivot.

![The Student $t$ density with 1, 3 and 10 degrees of freedom, against the standard normal. Fewer degrees of freedom mean heavier tails, and therefore larger quantiles and wider intervals. By 10 degrees of freedom the curve is already close to normal.](../figures/inf-t-densities.pdf){#fig-inf-t-densities}

Placing $T$ between $\pm t_{n-1;1-\alpha/2}$ and solving for $\mu$ gives the interval

$$
\overline X\pm t_{n-1;\,1-\alpha/2}\,\frac{s}{\sqrt n},
$$

where $t_{m;q}$ is the quantile of order $q$ of the $t$ distribution with $m$ degrees of freedom. For large $n$ this quantile is close to the corresponding normal quantile, because $s$ is then close to $\sigma$.

::: {#exm-household-fuel-spending .example}
## Household fuel spending

An oil company samples 51 households at random from a city. They spent on average $\overline x=1136$ dollars a year on petrol and heating oil, with bias-corrected standard deviation $s=178$ dollars.

**Question.** Give a 95% confidence interval for the mean spending $\mu$ in the city, and say what the model assumes.

**Solution.** Model the spending of the 51 households as a random sample from $\Normal(\mu,\sigma^2)$, both unknown. Random selection justifies independence and a common distribution. Normality is an assumption; with $n=51$ the central limit theorem makes it matter little for an interval about the mean. With $t_{50;0.975}=2.009$, the standard error is $178/\sqrt{51}=24.93$, and

$$
1136\pm2.009\times24.93=1136\pm50.1=(1085.9,\ 1186.1).
$$

:::

### A variance

The variance uses the chi-squared pivot $(n-1)s^2/\sigma^2$, which is $\chi^2_{n-1}$ by the normal sample theorem. Writing $\chi^2_{m;q}$ for its quantile of order $q$,

$$
\Pr\Bigl(\chi^2_{n-1;\,\alpha/2}<\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma^2}<\chi^2_{n-1;\,1-\alpha/2}\Bigr)=1-\alpha.
$$

Solving for $\sigma^2$ gives the confidence interval

$$
\left(\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{n-1;\,1-\alpha/2}},\;\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{n-1;\,\alpha/2}}\right).
$$

The upper quantile sits in the lower endpoint, because the pivot has $\sigma^2$ in the denominator. The chi-squared law is skewed, so the interval is not symmetric about $s^2$. An interval for $\sigma$ is found by taking square roots of both endpoints; a monotone function carries the coverage with it.

::: {#exm-aspirin-tablet-weights .example}
## Aspirin tablet weights

A label states that tablet weights have standard deviation 1.0 mg. A sample of 25 tablets has $s=1.3$ mg.

**Question.** Give 95% confidence intervals for $\sigma^2$ and for $\sigma$, assuming normal weights. Is the label believable?

**Solution.** With 24 degrees of freedom, $\chi^2_{24;0.025}=12.40$ and $\chi^2_{24;0.975}=39.36$. Since $(n-1)s^2=24\times1.69=40.56$,

$$
\left(\frac{40.56}{39.36},\ \frac{40.56}{12.40}\right)=(1.03,\ 3.27)
$$

for $\sigma^2$, and $(1.02,\ 1.81)$ mg for $\sigma$. The interval for $\sigma$ excludes the stated $1.0$ mg, so the data cast doubt on the label at the 95% level.

:::

## Two normal samples

Let the first sample have size $n_1$, mean $\overline X_1$ and variance $s_1^2$, and the second sample size $n_2$, mean $\overline X_2$ and variance $s_2^2$. The samples are independent, the first is $\Normal(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)$, and the second is $\Normal(\mu_2,\sigma_2^2)$.

### A difference of means

The construction is like the one-sample case, with one extra assumption: the two variances are equal, $\sigma_1^2=\sigma_2^2=\sigma^2$. Then

$$
\frac{(\overline X_1-\overline X_2)-(\mu_1-\mu_2)}{\sigma\sqrt{1/n_1+1/n_2}}
$$

is standard normal, and the common variance is estimated by pooling.

::: {#def-pooled-variance .definition}
## Pooled variance

For two independent samples assumed to share a variance $\sigma^2$, the pooled sample variance is

$$
s_p^2=\frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2}.
$$

It is unbiased for $\sigma^2$, and $(n_1+n_2-2)s_p^2/\sigma^2$ is $\chi^2_{n_1+n_2-2}$.

:::

The pooled variance weights each sample variance by its degrees of freedom. The chi-squared statement holds because $(n_1-1)s_1^2/\sigma^2$ and $(n_2-1)s_2^2/\sigma^2$ are independent $\chi^2_{n_1-1}$ and $\chi^2_{n_2-1}$ variables, and independent chi-squared variables add their degrees of freedom.

::: {#thm-two-sample-t-pivot .theorem}
## Two-sample t pivot

For two independent normal samples with a common variance,

$$
T=\frac{(\overline X_1-\overline X_2)-(\mu_1-\mu_2)}{s_p\sqrt{1/n_1+1/n_2}}
$$

has a $t$ distribution with $n_1+n_2-2$ degrees of freedom.

:::

The proof is the one-sample argument again. The numerator over $\sigma\sqrt{1/n_1+1/n_2}$ is standard normal, the pooled chi-squared variable is $(n_1+n_2-2)s_p^2/\sigma^2$, and the two are independent because each sample mean is independent of its own sample variance and the samples are independent of each other. The resulting interval for $\mu_1-\mu_2$ is

$$
\overline X_1-\overline X_2\pm t_{n_1+n_2-2;\,1-\alpha/2}\;s_p\sqrt{\frac1{n_1}+\frac1{n_2}}.
$$

For the safety measures, $n_1=n_2=50$, the estimate is $-17$, the standard error is $2.84$, and $t_{98;0.975}=1.984$. The 95% interval is

$$
-17\pm1.984\times2.84=-17\pm5.64=(-22.6,\ -11.4).
$$

It lies wholly below zero. The interval $-17\pm2.84$, one standard error each side, would have coverage of only about 68%.

### A ratio of variances

The pooled interval is valid only if the variances are equal. That can be checked with an interval for $\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2$, and seeing whether it contains 1.

::: {#thm-variance-ratio-f-pivot .theorem}
## Variance-ratio F pivot

For two independent normal samples,

$$
\frac{s_1^2/\sigma_1^2}{s_2^2/\sigma_2^2}
$$

has the $F$ distribution with $(n_1-1,\,n_2-1)$ degrees of freedom.

:::

Write $U=(n_1-1)s_1^2/\sigma_1^2$ and $V=(n_2-1)s_2^2/\sigma_2^2$. These are independent $\chi^2_{n_1-1}$ and $\chi^2_{n_2-1}$ variables, and the ratio is $\{U/(n_1-1)\}/\{V/(n_2-1)\}$, which is the definition of $F_{n_1-1,n_2-1}$. Placing the pivot between its quantiles and using $1/F_{m_1,m_2;\,\alpha/2}=F_{m_2,m_1;\,1-\alpha/2}$ gives the interval

$$
\left(\frac{1}{F_{n_1-1,n_2-1;\,1-\alpha/2}}\,\frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2},\ \ F_{n_2-1,n_1-1;\,1-\alpha/2}\,\frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2}\right).
$$

For the safety measures, $s_1^2/s_2^2=14.1^2/14.3^2=0.972$ and $F_{49,49;0.975}=1.762$, so the 95% interval for $\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2$ is $(0.552,\ 1.713)$. It contains 1, so there is no reason at the 5% level to doubt the equal-variance assumption behind the pooled interval.

## A proportion

Let $X\sim\Bin(n,p)$ and $\widehat p=X/n$. An exact interval is awkward because the binomial law is discrete. For large $n$ the central limit theorem gives

$$
\frac{\widehat p-p}{\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}}\approx\Normal(0,1),
$$

so $\Pr(-z_{1-\alpha/2}<(\widehat p-p)/\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}<z_{1-\alpha/2})\approx1-\alpha$. Solving for $p$ leaves $p$ inside the standard error. For large $n$, $\widehat p$ is close to $p$, and replacing the unknown standard error by $\sqrt{\widehat p(1-\widehat p)/n}$ produces an interval whose ends depend only on the data.

::: {#def-wald-interval .definition}
## Wald interval

For $X\sim\Bin(n,p)$ with $\widehat p=X/n$, the Wald interval with approximate confidence $1-\alpha$ is

$$
\widehat p\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\widehat p(1-\widehat p)}{n}}.
$$

:::

It is an approximation. It behaves badly when $n$ is small or $\widehat p$ is near $0$ or $1$, because the estimated standard error is then a poor stand-in and the normal shape has not set in. At $\widehat p=0$ it collapses to a single point. A common rule is to use it only when $n\widehat p$ and $n(1-\widehat p)$ are both at least 5. It also models the sample as independent draws: a poll with refusals or untruthful answers has errors no interval formula can see.

For two independent samples the same approximation applies to $\widehat p_1-\widehat p_2$, whose variance is the sum of the two variances. The interval is

$$
\widehat p_1-\widehat p_2\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\widehat p_1(1-\widehat p_1)}{n_1}+\frac{\widehat p_2(1-\widehat p_2)}{n_2}}.
$$

::: {#exm-nightmares-in-two-groups .example}
## Nightmares in two groups

Of 160 men, 55 report frequent nightmares; of 192 women, 60 do.

**Question.** Give an approximate 95% confidence interval for the difference $p_1-p_2$ in the population proportions, and interpret it.

**Solution.** $\widehat p_1=55/160=0.344$ and $\widehat p_2=60/192=0.313$, a difference of $0.031$. The standard error is

$$
\sqrt{\frac{0.344\times0.656}{160}+\frac{0.313\times0.688}{192}}=0.0503,
$$

so the interval is $0.031\pm1.96\times0.0503=(-0.067,\ 0.130)$. It contains 0. The data are consistent with no difference between men and women, and also with a difference of several percentage points either way.

:::

## How large a sample?

For a normal mean with known $\sigma$, the half-width of the interval is $E=z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\sigma/\sqrt n$. Solving for $n$, a half-width of at most $E$ needs

$$
n\ge\Bigl(\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\sigma}{E}\Bigr)^2.
$$

Halving the half-width needs four times the sample. For a proportion the same calculation with $\sigma^2=p(1-p)\le1/4$ gives the conservative $n\ge z_{1-\alpha/2}^2/(4E^2)$. A poll accurate to $\pm3$ percentage points with 95% confidence needs about $1.96^2/(4\times0.03^2)\approx1068$ people, whatever the size of the population.

::: {.callout-note}
## Key idea
A confidence interval is a pivot solved for the parameter. The coverage probability is computed before the data are seen, over all the samples that might have been drawn. The numerical interval reported afterwards is not assigned that probability.
:::

## A proportion in a poll

In a sample of 1000 registered voters, 227 say they will vote for a given party. Using the Wald approximation and $z_{0.975}=1.960$, give an approximate 95% confidence interval for the population proportion.

[Solution](#sol-inf-green-voters)

:::

::: {#ex-inf-mean-pivot .exercise}
## The interval for a normal mean

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent and $\Normal(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma$ unknown. Starting from the $t$ pivot $(\overline X-\mu)/(s/\sqrt n)$, derive the confidence interval for $\mu$ with confidence $1-\alpha$.

[Solution](#sol-inf-mean-pivot)

:::

::: {#ex-inf-two-standard-errors .exercise}
## Two standard errors

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent and $\Normal(\mu,1)$. Find the exact coverage of the interval $\overline X\pm 2/\sqrt n$, and the multiplier $c$ for which $\overline X\pm c/\sqrt n$ has coverage exactly 99%.

[Solution](#sol-inf-two-standard-errors)

:::

::: {#ex-inf-safety-interval .exercise}
## Lost hours after a safety programme

Lost working hours averaged 91 per month over 50 months after a safety programme, with standard deviation 14.1, and 108 per month over the 50 months before, with standard deviation 14.3. Assume two independent normal samples with a common variance.

(a) Compute the pooled standard deviation and a 95% confidence interval for $\mu_1-\mu_2$. Use $t_{98;0.975}=1.984$.

(b) Someone reports the result as $-17\pm2.84$. What coverage does that interval have?

[Solution](#sol-inf-safety-interval)

:::

::: {#ex-inf-variance-ratio-interval .exercise}
## Checking equal variances

For the two samples in the previous exercise, give a 95% confidence interval for $\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2$, using $F_{49,49;0.975}=1.762$. Does it support pooling?

[Solution](#sol-inf-variance-ratio-interval)

:::

::: {#ex-inf-poll-size .exercise}
## Sizing a poll

How many voters should a poll sample so that the 95% Wald interval for a proportion has half-width at most $0.02$, whatever the true proportion? How does the answer change if earlier polls show the proportion is near $0.1$?

[Solution](#sol-inf-poll-size)
